body_html:
The best books to learn Spanish are not the ones with the most stars on Amazon. They are the ones that match where you are right now and what is actually holding you back. Over the years, as a learner and then as an English–Spanish translator, I have used every book on this list, and I still recommend them to friends. Below are my honest picks for beginners and early intermediates, grouped by the job each book does best, plus my own bilingual books, which I have marked clearly so you can judge them for yourself.

Quick answer
  • Best all-in-one course book: Complete Latin American Spanish (Teach Yourself)
  • Best grammar workbook for beginners: Easy Spanish Step-by-Step
  • Best first reader: Short Stories in Spanish for Beginners
  • Best for reading something meaningful early: bilingual books, including my own
  • Start with one course book, one workbook and one reader, not a pile of ten books.
{{toc}}

How to choose the best books to learn Spanish

Most beginners make the same mistake I made: they buy five books, start all of them and finish none. A better approach is to choose one book for each job:

  • A course book gives you structure: what to learn, in what order.
  • A grammar workbook gives you practice: exercises that make the rules automatic.
  • A reader gives you real Spanish: stories or texts that build vocabulary and confidence.

Pick one of each from the list below, use them together for a few months, and only then add more. Here is the short version:

PickBest forLevel
Complete Latin American Spanish (Teach Yourself)A full self-study courseA1–B1
Easy Spanish Step-by-StepGrammar with exercisesA1–A2
Madrigal’s Magic Key to SpanishUsing cognates to start fastA1
Practice Makes Perfect: Complete Spanish GrammarDrilling grammarA2–B1
Short Stories in Spanish for BeginnersA first readerA2–B1
Breaking Out of Beginner’s SpanishSounding naturalB1
My bilingual booksMeaningful reading with Spanish woven inA2–B2

The best course book

1. Complete Latin American Spanish (Teach Yourself)

Best for: learners who want one book that covers everything · Level: A1–B1

If you only buy one book, make it a complete course. Complete Latin American Spanish takes you from greetings to the past tenses in a clear sequence, with dialogues, grammar explanations, exercises and audio, using the Spanish you will hear across Latin America and in the United States. What I like most is that each unit builds on the last, so you always know what to study next.

What to know: it is a textbook, so it can feel slow if you prefer stories. Pair it with a reader to keep motivation up.

See it on Amazon →

The best grammar books for beginners

2. Easy Spanish Step-by-Step

Best for: beginners who want grammar explained simply, with practice · Level: A1–A2

Barbara Bregstein’s book introduces grammar in small steps, and each new chapter reuses what came before, so you are constantly practicing. It is the book I would give someone who feels lost with verb endings. The exercises are short enough to do in fifteen minutes.

What to know: the reading passages are simple and functional rather than exciting.

See it on Amazon →

3. Practice Makes Perfect: Complete Spanish Grammar

Best for: learners who learn by doing exercises · Level: A2–B1

Gilda Nissenberg’s workbook is pure practice: short explanations followed by pages of exercises, with an answer key. It covers everything from the present tense to double object pronouns. I still think it is one of the best ways to make grammar automatic.

What to know: it is a workbook, not a course, so use it alongside something that teaches you the basics first. For more grammar options, see my list of the {{link:best-spanish-grammar-books|best Spanish grammar books}}.

See it on Amazon →

4. Madrigal’s Magic Key to Spanish

Best for: complete beginners who want quick confidence · Level: A1

Margarita Madrigal’s classic starts from words you already know because they look like English, and builds sentences from them right away. It is old-fashioned in places, but it gives beginners an early feeling of “I can do this”, which matters more than people think. It pairs well with my guide to {{link:english-spanish-cognates|English–Spanish cognates}}.

What to know: some examples feel dated, and it doesn’t replace a full course.

See it on Amazon →

{{image:2}}

The best first readers

5. Short Stories in Spanish for Beginners

Best for: your first real reading in Spanish · Level: A2–B1

Olly Richards’ graded readers are short stories written for learners, with vocabulary lists, summaries and comprehension questions after each chapter. They are the books I recommend most often to people who have finished a few months of study and want to start reading. There is also a second volume when you finish the first.

What to know: the stories are written for learners, so the language is simpler than real books. That is the point at this stage. For more on how to read at this level, see {{link:reading-in-spanish-for-beginners|reading in Spanish for beginners}}.

See it on Amazon →

6. Breaking Out of Beginner’s Spanish

Best for: learners stuck at the “textbook Spanish” stage · Level: B1

Joseph Keenan’s book is about the gap between correct Spanish and natural Spanish: the expressions, false friends and habits that textbooks skip. It is funny, opinionated and full of the kind of detail I deal with as a translator every day.

What to know: it is a book to read, not a course. Come back to it once you have the basics. My guides to {{link:spanish-false-friends|Spanish false friends}} and {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes}} cover similar ground.

See it on Amazon →

Bilingual books, including my own

Disclosure: the three books in this section are mine. I include them because they fill a gap I saw for years, but I am obviously not neutral, so read the description and decide for yourself.

Graded readers are great, but they are stories written to teach vocabulary. Many adult learners also want to read something that speaks to their own life while they learn. That is why I wrote my bilingual books: each one holds 300 short pages written in English with natural Spanish woven in, plus a Spanish Note that explains idioms, false friends and everyday usage. You always understand the meaning, so the Spanish has room to land. I explain the method in {{link:parallel-text-reading|parallel text reading}}.

7. A Road in Bloom | Un camino en flor

Best for: reflective readers who want Spanish about real life · Level: A2–B2

300 bilingual truths about love, family, friendship, money and growing up. I wrote about why in {{link:a-road-in-bloom|A Road in Bloom: why I wrote a bilingual book on growing up}}.

See it on Amazon →

8. Love, Slowly | Amor, despacio

Best for: learners who want the Spanish of feelings and relationships · Level: A2–B2

300 bilingual truths about crushes, heartbreak and choosing yourself, with “Love Note” pages worth sharing. More in {{link:love-slowly|the story behind Love, Slowly}}.

See it on Amazon →

9. The Mind Lies | La mente miente

Best for: curious readers who like psychology · Level: A2–B2

300 bilingual psychology truths about overthinking, habits and fear, each with a Spanish Note. More in {{link:the-mind-lies|why I wrote The Mind Lies}}.

See it on Amazon →

{{image:3}}

A simple plan for your first three months

  1. Weeks 1–4: one unit of your course book every two or three days, plus fifteen minutes of a workbook.
  2. Weeks 5–8: keep the course and workbook, and add one or two pages of a reader or a bilingual book every day.
  3. Weeks 9–12: start listening too; my list of the {{link:best-spanish-podcasts|best Spanish podcasts}} has options for every level.

Books work best with a little daily contact with real Spanish. Apps and podcasts can fill that gap; see the {{link:best-apps-to-learn-spanish|best apps to learn Spanish}}. And keep a good dictionary close: my {{link:best-spanish-dictionary|favorite Spanish dictionaries}} are the ones I use for work.

Books I would skip as a beginner

  • Big reference grammars like A New Reference Grammar of Modern Spanish. Excellent, but they are for later.
  • Phrasebooks as your main book. They help on a trip, but they won’t teach you how Spanish works.
  • Classic novels in Spanish too early. Reading Cien años de soledad at A2 is a fast way to give up. Build up with readers first.
{{if:easy-spanish-stories}}

For free reading practice, start with my {{link:easy-spanish-stories|easy Spanish stories}}, each with the English underneath.

{{/if}}

Final thoughts

The best books to learn Spanish are the ones you will open every day. Choose one course book, one workbook and one reader, give them three months, and you will be surprised how far you get. If you want reading that also means something, I hope you will give my bilingual books a try, and tell me honestly what you think on Goodreads.

faq.q: What is the best book to learn Spanish for beginners?
faq.a: For an all-in-one course, Complete Latin American Spanish (Teach Yourself). For grammar with exercises, Easy Spanish Step-by-Step. Most beginners do best with one of each plus a reader.

faq.q: Can I learn Spanish from books alone?
faq.a: Books give you structure and reading practice, but you also need listening and speaking. Combine them with podcasts, apps or a tutor.

faq.q: How many books do I need to learn Spanish?
faq.a: Start with three: a course book, a grammar workbook and a reader. Add more only when you finish one.

faq.q: Are bilingual books good for learning Spanish?
faq.a: Yes, especially for adults. Seeing the meaning in English while reading the Spanish makes new language easier to understand and remember.

faq.q: When should I start reading in Spanish?
faq.a: After a few months of basics, start with graded readers or bilingual books at your level, then move to real books later.
